name: basement-worms-eye
prompt: Portrait frame shot from the concrete floor of a windowless council records basement, the camera lying almost flat on scuffed grey lino and tilted steeply upward through a 14mm ultra-wide lens, so the scene leans inward and towers. Filling the centre and climbing straight out of the top of the frame is one colossal column of loose office paper, thousands of sheets squared into a slab taller than any room should allow, its edges slightly ragged and yellowed. A plain white paper band wrapped round the stack at head height carries bold black condensed sans-serif capitals reading "THE RULES", sharp and correctly spelled. Five people stand at its base in a loose ring, heads tilted far back, staring up: one in a navy hoodie, one in a black puffer jacket, one in an orange hi-vis vest over a grey fleece, one in a charcoal work jacket, one in an olive parka. Each wears a full cloth balaclava in a different dark colour (maroon, bottle green, slate, black, deep navy) covering the whole head with no openings for eyes, nose or mouth, the hem tucked into the collar; a thick white ring is stitched round the whole face, and a small red triangle sits high inside the ring over the wearer's left eye, toward the two o'clock position. Every hand is in a black work glove with the jacket cuff pulled over the wrist; no skin anywhere. Grey steel archive shelving packed with box files recedes on both sides into gloom. The only light falls from a row of bare fluorescent tubes far overhead, one of them stuttering, giving a cold mercury green-white cast that leaves the clothing murky and dull while the white rings and red triangles catch it and glow. Deep focus from the nearest boot to the furthest sheet, hard flat shadows, slight noise, the matter-of-fact grain of a phone photo taken in a forgotten room.

name: parr-flash-council-office
prompt: Portrait-format documentary photograph, midday, inside the reception of a tired modern British district council office. Magnolia walls scuffed at hip height, a long laminate counter in fake beech with a peeling edge strip, a red take-a-number dispenser on a chrome pole with a paper tongue sticking out, a perspex leaflet rack of sun-faded flyers on recycling and council tax, a row of bolted orange plastic chairs, a sad yucca in a pot, carpet tiles in municipal grey. Five figures queue in a tidy line in front of the counter, shoulders slumped like people who have been here an hour, every head tipped back to stare upward. Behind the counter, crammed wall to wall, rises an enormous heap of printed paper, dog-eared and bulging, which bursts through the suspended ceiling where one square tile has been knocked loose and dangles from the grid; taped to the heap at eye level is one laminated A4 sheet printed in plain black capitals: THE RULES. Each of the five wears a knitted balaclava in a loud colour that clashes with the next: lime green, bubblegum pink, traffic-cone orange, cobalt blue, egg-yolk yellow. Their faces are smooth solid knit from brow to chin, featureless cloth where eyes, nose and mouth would be. A thick white stitched circle frames the whole front of each head, and high inside it, on the wearer's left side so it lands on the viewer's right near two o'clock, a red triangle with softened corners is sewn on, never centred. Below the hoods: a shiny polyester tracksuit, a cheap rain anorak, a puffer jacket, collars zipped up over the neck, sleeves pulled past the wrists, cotton gloves on both hands of every figure, not a scrap of skin anywhere. The figure at the front of the queue holds a small numbered ticket between gloved fingers. Shot straight on at chest height with a wide-angle lens from a few steps back, deep focus, the frame stuffed with clutter to every edge. Lit by one hard flash fired from the camera into daylight, so the colours of the knitwear and plastic come out saturated and slightly garish, a glossy glare bounces off the counter, crisp dark cast-shadows sit on the wall behind each figure, and the room's corners fall off a touch darker. Palette and texture of slow colour-negative film from a high-street minilab: over-bright, a little cheap, fine grain. Deadpan, unstaged, quietly absurd.

name: crewdson-terrace-blue-hour
prompt: Portrait-format staged photograph of an ordinary British terraced street just after sunset, shot from the middle of the road on a tripod at chest height with a moderate wide lens, camera tipped slightly up. Red-brick two-up two-down houses run away on both sides: white uPVC doors, small front walls, black and green wheelie bins out for collection, a grey hatchback and a small red one parked nose to tail, a dripping drainpipe, wet tarmac with a faint sheen. Blocking the street from kerb to kerb and climbing level with the chimney pots is one enormous stack of white A4 paper, neatly squared, its edges slightly ragged, the uppermost sheet's front edge stencilled in bold black block letters reading THE RULES. At its foot, filling only the bottom third of the frame and dwarfed by it, five gang members stand spaced in an uneven line with their heads craned back, mostly seen from behind, the two at the ends turned enough that we see their masks. They wear what people wear on a British estate today: a black puffer jacket, a grey zip-up fleece, a navy tracksuit, an olive parka with the hood down, a burgundy bomber, white trainers. Every head is covered by a fitted cloth balaclava, each a different colour (charcoal, bottle green, royal blue, ochre, black), with no openings for eyes, nose or mouth; a broad white stitched circle frames the whole face, and inside it a single red triangle with rounded corners sits high on the wearer's own left side, which from the camera reads as the two o'clock position, clearly off-centre. Balaclavas tuck down inside zipped-up collars; both hands of every figure are in dark gloves, sleeves pulled over the wrists, no skin visible at all; plain fabric, nothing metallic or electronic. Light is arranged like a film set: tall sodium streetlamps pour amber cones onto the pavement, each terrace window glows a different warm shade through net curtains, one upstairs bedroom lamp is on, and a single hard, cool white floodlight from low and off to the left rakes upward across the paper face so the lettering and every sheet's edge read crisp. Above the roofline the sky is a saturated, cloudless cobalt blue; beneath it the street is bathed in warm orange, a clean split of cold sky and warm ground. Empty, silent, unsettling, as if the whole neighbourhood is holding its breath. Deep focus from the gang to the top of the stack, natural photographic detail, gentle grain, no other words or signage visible anywhere.

name: profile-close-window-light
prompt: Photorealistic vertical close-up portrait, framed from the top of the shoulders to just above the crown, made on an 85mm lens at f/1.8 so only the wool is sharp. A masked figure is turned three-quarters, the left side of their head toward the camera, chin lifted and throat stretched as they stare up at something enormous above them. The whole head is covered by a charcoal balaclava of chunky cable-knit yarn, its face a smooth, unbroken expanse of wool, no holes cut anywhere for sight, breath or speech. A thick band of white yarn is sewn in a full circle around the face. Within that circle, set high in its upper-right arc as the viewer sees it, directly over where the left eye would be, sits a small red felt triangle with softened corners, plainly off to one side, never central. The lower edge of the knit disappears inside the raised corduroy collar of an olive waxed cotton jacket, and a black knitted glove holds the collar closed, the sleeve cuff covering the wrist so no skin shows at all. A low late-afternoon sun pours through an unseen window on the left, a warm honey-coloured shaft that rakes across the wool, lighting every loop and loose fibre and leaving the far cheek in soft brown shadow. Behind and above the figure, dissolved into creamy blur, a towering wall of stacked paper reams and bundled documents fills the top half of the frame in cool bluish white; one sheet near the figure's line of sight shows a bold black printed heading, THE RULES, readable through the softness. Palette of warm amber and charcoal against cold paper white, fine film grain, an everyday room in present-day Britain, only cloth and paper, nothing shiny, metallic or lit up.

name: overhead-from-the-top
prompt: Vertical 9:16 night photograph shot from the summit of a giant column of piled office paper, the lens pointing ninety degrees straight down its side. In the bottom-near foreground the top page lies flat under the camera, perfectly sharp, printed with THE RULES in heavy black block capitals. Beyond its edge the stack falls away as a sheer pale wall of compressed page edges, converging steeply in an ultra-wide 16mm perspective to a puddled concrete warehouse floor far below. Down there five small figures, a little soft, stand close together with their heads thrown back so their faces point up at us. They wear ordinary clothes from a British high street this year: a hoodie under a puffer jacket, a hi-vis work vest, a black rain shell, joggers, trainers and boots, thick gloves on both hands with sleeves pulled over the wrists, collars zipped up to the jaw. Over every head is a close wool hood, blank where a face should be, and every hood is its own deep shade: navy, bottle green, charcoal, oxblood, black. Sewn onto each hood is a broad white hoop that encircles the face, and within that hoop one red triangle is placed up near the top of the hoop on the side of the wearer's left eye socket, so to us it shows on the right-hand side of the mask, never in the middle. Only wool and stitching, nothing hard or glowing. The figures hold small torches aimed up the paper cliff, and nothing else in the room is bright: the beams cut pale shafts through floating dust, throwing white blooms onto the page edges and making the white rings and red triangles flash. A weak orange sodium haze leaks in from a tiny window high on the far wall and touches one flank of the stack. Beyond those beams the warehouse drowns in black, with wet glints on the floor. Night, high contrast, visible film grain, a dizzying drop seen from the top.

name: high-key-white-monolith
prompt: Tall portrait photograph of a boundless white infinity cove, floor sweeping up into the back wall in one soft curve so there is no corner and no horizon, bathed in even, wraparound softbox light from every direction: no cast shadows, only a pale contact shadow under each trainer. In the exact middle of the frame rises one towering slab of stacked office paper, crisp and rectangular as a plinth of white marble, its edges showing thousands of fine sheet lines, its top nearly touching the upper edge of the picture. At its foot sits a small gallery wall card printed with THE RULES in neat black sans-serif capitals. Lined up in front of it, tiny against the slab, stand four people in a tidy row, bodies turned three-quarters away from us, heads tipped back to stare up its height. Each wears a bright hand-knitted balaclava in its own loud colour, hot pink, lime green, cobalt blue, tangerine, the knit closed over the whole face, solid wool where eyes, nose and mouth would be. The person second from the right has turned to look back at the lens, showing the mask front: a wide white knitted ring outlining the face, and inside it, high up toward the upper right of the picture, a small red triangle with rounded corners stitched over the wearer's left eye, never in the centre. The others show the edge of the same red triangle on their turned heads. Plain, current UK clothing in black and slate grey: zip hoodie, bomber jacket, puffer gilet, joggers, white-soled trainers; the knit tucked into every collar; black gloves on all hands, sleeves pulled over the wrists, no bare skin anywhere. Shot from far back at chest height on a long lens, perfectly level and mirror-symmetrical, motionless and calm. Colour: white on white with faint silver-grey tones; the knitted masks and their red triangles are the only saturated colour in the picture. Hushed, clean, exhibition-quiet, high-key.
